short: Created by Augustus in 2 BCE to command his guard, the praetorian prefecture became, by the fourth century, the empire's senior civil office.
full:
Augustus established the office of praetorian prefect in 2 BCE, appointing two equestrian officers jointly to command his personal guard so that no single man held that force alone. Later prefects, most notoriously Sejanus under Tiberius, accumulated wide-ranging authority over the imperial court, and by the third century the office had also absorbed judicial and financial responsibilities across the empire.

Constantine stripped the prefecture of military command after 312, replacing it with new military masters, the magistri militum, and split it into regional prefectures, Gaul, Italy and Africa, Illyricum, and the East, each responsible for civil administration, taxation and justice across its dioceses. Purely civilian from then on, the praetorian prefecture remained the highest tier of Roman administration below the emperor for the rest of the empire's history.
